title: LoRA and QLoRA: Fine-Tuning a Large Model on One GPU

images.caption: QLoRA (2023) fine-tuned a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU and preserved 16-bit fine-tuning performance; Guanaco reached 99.3% of ChatGPT on Vicuna after 24 hours. The full fine-tuning bar is a byte-count estimate.

images.target_after_text_full: For comparison, full fine-tuning in the usual way needs roughly 16 bytes of GPU memory per parameter, about 1 TB for a 65B model, before counting activations. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate from byte counts.
images.next_text: QLoRA combines two parts: LoRA reduces the number of parameters that are trained, and 4-bit quantization reduces the nu...
images.next_text_full: QLoRA combines two parts: LoRA reduces the number of parameters that are trained, and 4-bit quantization reduces the number of bits each parameter takes. Three basic concepts explain both: rank, low-rank approximation and quantization. One idea connects them all: the pattern in a matrix.
images.target_block_html: For comparison, full fine-tuning in the usual way needs roughly 16 bytes of GPU memory per parameter, about 1 TB for a 65B model, before counting activations. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate from byte counts.

images.caption: LoRA freezes W and trains only B·A, a sum of r patterns, starting from B = 0. After training, B·A can be merged into W.
images.target_after_text: After training, B·A has the same shape as W, so it can be added into W with no extra cost at inference. Alternatively,...
images.target_after_text_full: After training, B·A has the same shape as W, so it can be added into W with no extra cost at inference. Alternatively, different A and B can be kept for different tasks and swapped as needed. The LoRA paper reports that, on GPT-3 175B, it reduces trainable parameters by about 10,000 times and GPU memory needs by about 3 times compared with full fine-tuning with Adam.
images.next_text: LoRA has limits. The rank r bounds what the update can express: a change that needs more than r patterns can't be learn...
images.next_text_full: LoRA has limits. The rank r bounds what the update can express: a change that needs more than r patterns can't be learned completely. And LoRA reduces only the training state; the original weights still sit in GPU memory at 16 bits. For a 65B model, the weights alone take about 130 GB.
images.target_block_html: After training, B·A has the same shape as W, so it can be added into W with no extra cost at inference. Alternatively, different A and B can be kept for different tasks and swapped as needed. The LoRA paper reports that, on GPT-3 175B, it reduces trainable parameters by about 10,000 times and GPU memory needs by about 3 times compared with full fine-tuning with Adam.

images.caption: 4-bit quantization of one block: divide by the block scale, snap to the nearest of 16 levels, store the 4-bit code.
images.target_after_text: Block-wise scaling. The 16 levels lie between −1 and 1, while real weights are small, often within about ±0.05. So the...
images.target_after_text_full: Block-wise scaling. The 16 levels lie between −1 and 1, while real weights are small, often within about ±0.05. So the weights are split into blocks of 64, and each block stores one scale: the largest absolute weight in the block. To store a weight, divide it by the scale, find the nearest level and keep its index. To use it, multiply the level by the scale. With blocks, an unusually large weight affects only its own block.
images.next_text: NF4. QLoRA uses a 4-bit format called NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat). Trained weights are roughly bell-shaped, so NF4 places i...
images.next_text_full: NF4. QLoRA uses a 4-bit format called NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat). Trained weights are roughly bell-shaped, so NF4 places its 16 levels at quantiles of the normal distribution: dense near 0, sparse in the tails, with an exact 0. Most weights sit near 0, so their rounding error is smaller.

images.target_after_text_full: NF4. QLoRA uses a 4-bit format called NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat). Trained weights are roughly bell-shaped, so NF4 places its 16 levels at quantiles of the normal distribution: dense near 0, sparse in the tails, with an exact 0. Most weights sit near 0, so their rounding error is smaller.
images.next_text: Storage and compute. Each weight takes 4 bits, plus a share of the scale used by its block of 64. Quantizing the scales...
images.next_text_full: Storage and compute. Each weight takes 4 bits, plus a share of the scale used by its block of 64. Quantizing the scales themselves to 8 bits, called double quantization, brings the average to about 4.13 bits per weight, roughly a quarter of bf16. At compute time, each block is converted back to bf16 just before its matrix multiplication and discarded afterward: storage is 4-bit, computation is still 16-bit.
images.target_block_html: NF4. QLoRA uses a 4-bit format called NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat). Trained weights are roughly bell-shaped, so NF4 places its 16 levels at quantiles of the normal distribution: dense near 0, sparse in the tails, with an exact 0. Most weights sit near 0, so their rounding error is smaller.

images.caption: Low rank removes the weak patterns; quantization keeps every pattern and adds a small, spread-out error.
images.target_after_text: This explains an apparent contradiction. Pretrained weights are hard to compress with low rank, because they contain ma...
images.target_after_text_full: This explains an apparent contradiction. Pretrained weights are hard to compress with low rank, because they contain many patterns and dropping the weak ones loses much information. They can still be quantized well, because all patterns are kept and only a little noise is added.

images.next_text_full: The costs of QLoRA: converting weights before every computation makes training slower than 16-bit LoRA; quantization adds a little error, so the quantized model starts slightly worse and LoRA must make up for it during training; and the trained A and B can't simply be added into 4-bit weights, so they are merged into a 16-bit copy or kept separate.
images.target_block_html: A rough byte-count estimate for a 7B model, counting weights, gradients and optimizer state but not activations: about 100 GB for full fine-tuning, about 15 GB for LoRA and about 5 GB for QLoRA.
